prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms are held at the magic wavelength, bringing the measurement of time and frequency to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, the optical lattice clock, credited to Katori and Ye. The chair asked what the atomic physicists can cite beyond better accuracy, and what separates this from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. My answer is this. The comb made optical frequencies countable, and the 2012 work showed how to control one ion. Neither says that a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be held in a standing wave of light with the trap shifting both clock levels by the same amount, so that the trap drops out of the measurement. That is a statement about atomic polarisabilities, and it was a proposal that could be checked by calculation before it was demonstrated. What came after is physics and not only engineering. Many-atom clocks at the 1e-18 level have resolved the gravitational redshift across about a millimetre, which means a laboratory sample now feels the curvature of time. They have also shown how interactions and collective effects among lattice atoms limit and then improve the clock, and they set bounds on drifts of fundamental constants and on dark-matter couplings. The result has been reproduced and surpassed at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, so it is not a single-laboratory claim. The credit is short and was proposed identically by all eight of us in the opening: Katori for the lattice concept and the first demonstrations, Ye for taking it to the accuracy and stability frontier. In round 1 I think I underplayed that second contribution. The best results depend on blackbody-radiation control, ultrastable lasers and the comb link, and Kroll is right that this is mostly Ye's work and not Katori's original idea. That is a reason for the pair, not for one name. I would not change the citation to name more people, because it is the invention and its realisation that we are crediting.
statement.case_against: The two honest reservations remain. First, this is closer to a discovery of a capability than of a phenomenon, and a committee that insists on the second could prefer topological insulators. Second, a two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams, who made decisive contributions to accuracy and stability, and the ion-clock lineage is a parallel path. I do not think the first reservation is fatal, since the gravitational-redshift and constants tests are about nature, but I cannot claim that the committee has no precedent problem if it decides that instrument-enabled measurement is not enough. On timing, I have heard the argument that we should wait for the redefinition of the second, and I do not accept it: the redefinition is a decision for the metrology community that follows from the performance, and the performance is already established. If the committee did decide to wait, I would not regard that as a scientific error, only as a different reading of how much a prize should anticipate. Last, I am an atomic theorist and I am inclined to find this field congenial, so I should discount my own enthusiasm.

responses.point: Kroll agrees with the pair and adds that the 1e-18 result owes much to blackbody-radiation control, ultrastable cavities and the comb link, mostly Ye's contribution. He proposes that the citation say explicitly that the achievement is the many-atom neutral lattice scheme, so that the committee is not seen as recognising timekeeping twice.
responses.response: I accept both points and have changed my citation because of them. In round 1 my wording said unprecedented accuracy in the measurement of time, which could be read as a general statement about clocks, and the ion clocks already have a claim there. The citation I now propose names the lattice, the neutral atoms and the magic wavelength, so the invention is the scheme and not the accuracy. I also agree that Ye's contribution is not a refinement of Katori's idea. The systematic control that took it to 1e-18 is a separate body of work, and it is the reason I want two names. Where I would qualify you slightly is that I would not call the Al+ ion clock a mere demonstration of the 2012 line. It is its own result, and that is why the wording must be about the many-atom lattice and not about being the best clock.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B007 above B056 and asks the committee to decide whether the lattice clock is a new capability built on recognised discoveries or a new physical discovery. He sees topological insulators as the cleaner discovery of new physics and keeps the clock as his first alternative.
responses.response: I take that distinction seriously, and I think the clock passes it for a specific reason. The comb and the ion control were both recognised for what they let us do. The magic-wavelength condition is a different kind of statement: it says that two atomic levels can be made to respond identically to a strong light field, which is a property of atomic structure that was not obvious and had to be worked out. I accept that B007 is a cleaner new phase of matter and I have kept it as my first alternative for that reason. The difficulty I still have is the one you share. Kane and Mele are credited for the theory and Molenkamp for the experiment, but the HgTe prediction came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and I cannot judge from outside condensed matter how much of the three-dimensional story the trio carries. If you and Mehlig can say that the quantum spin Hall effect separates cleanly from the 3D work, the gap between the two candidates narrows, but I still see a shorter and less contested credit line for the clock.

responses.point: Olsson argues that if B056 is accepted as an invention that opened up new measurements, B032 cannot easily be rejected as an instrument prize. She says either both count or neither does, and that B056 has more of its payoff still in the future.
responses.response: That is a fair test and I do not want to dodge it. I think the honest answer is that instrument prizes are legitimate when the instrument reaches a regime that changes what questions can be asked, and both candidates can claim that. I would not rank the clock above aberration correction simply because it is atomic physics. Where I see a difference is in what the instrument is used to learn. Aberration-corrected imaging mainly gives better pictures of known kinds of structure, though the pictures are remarkable, whereas the lattice clock is being used to test relativity at the millimetre scale and the constancy of constants. I also do not think the future payoff counts for the clock as you suggest. I would not rest the case on the redefinition of the second, and the results already in hand are enough. Given your flagged field closeness and the Nion line outside the trio, I think the committee will need a clean answer on Krivanek before B032 can be a serious competitor, and I do not think the primary record resolves that quickly.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B007 and regards it as a distinct, experimentally anchored achievement relative to the 2016 prize, while naming Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang as the main attribution risk. He also asks whether the clock is a new principle or superb instrumentation.
responses.response: On your last question, I would say new principle, and the principle is the magic wavelength. I would not call the rest superb instrumentation, because the control of interactions and blackbody shifts at the 1e-18 level is itself physics. As for B007, I find your argument that it is distinct from 2016 convincing and I have no objection to calling it mature. My difficulty is not with the science. It is that the three names have to carry a credit line that you yourself describe as incomplete, with Zhang no longer alive and unable to share it, and that makes the citation harder to defend than the clock's. If the committee wished to prefer B007 I could accept it as a sound choice, which is why I keep it as an alternative. I just do not see it as the stronger of the two on what we can state exactly in a citation.

responses.point: Pearce moved B056 from fifth to first on the strength of independent confirmation and short credit chain, but says he relies on Lindroth and Kroll for the atomic-physics details. He also accepts that IceCube is not settled enough to be first.
responses.response: I appreciate that you have asked us to supply the detail, so I will give the two points that matter most. The first is the physical condition: for a lattice at the magic wavelength the light shifts of the two clock states cancel, so that thousands of atoms are measured together without being disturbed by the trap. That was predicted and then confirmed, and it is why independent groups could rebuild the clock from the idea. The second is that the reproduction was not copying. SYRTE, PTB and NIST each used different species or different systematic controls and arrived at consistent frequency ratios, which is the kind of agreement between independent measurements that I would trust. I agree with you that IceCube is an excellent alternative and not yet the strongest first choice, and I would be happy to see it return when source identification settles.

responses.point: Johansson moved from circuit QED to the clock and says the line against the 2005 and 2012 prizes must be drawn carefully in the citation.
responses.response: I think we agree on the method. The line is drawn by naming what is new: neutral atoms, the lattice and the magic wavelength, and not the comb or ion control. I thank you for the move, but I would not want the committee to treat it as a defect that you opened elsewhere. I also want to repeat that I find circuit QED a real discovery, though I still see it as closer to the 2025 recognition than you do, and I do not think it should be weighed for this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as a discovery-level achievement and not as measurement capability, given that two members still prefer B007.
Whether Katori and Ye remain the fairest two names given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, which no citation wording can fully repair.
Whether the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang gap in B007 can be closed in a way that a condensed-matter colleague would call fair, since that decides how close the second candidate really is.
Whether recognition ahead of the SI redefinition of the second is accepted, which I regard as unnecessary to wait for but cannot show is the committee's view.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye has appeared in the discussion. I work in atomic theory and have long collaborated with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, none of which concerns B056. I have field closeness to B034 and B019, both of which I list only as alternatives or lower, and I would raise a recusal question if either became a leading candidate. I also noted that Olsson and Johansson have flagged closeness to their own preferred ballots, and I have no objection to how they have handled that.
